title: Skykraft's Board Hire Is a Signal That Space-Based ATC Communication Is Moving From Science Project to Commercial Bet
summary: The Australian startup's appointment of former FAA ATO chief Teri Bristol signals that satellite-based VHF communications for global ATM is crossing from demonstration phase into serious commercial deployment — and the implications for how pilots communicate over oceanic airspace are worth paying attention to.
body_markdown:
When a startup brings in someone like Teri Bristol — who ran the FAA's Air Traffic Organization, one of the largest and most complex air navigation service providers on the planet — it's not a routine board appointment. It's a signal about where the company thinks it is in its maturity arc and what doors it needs opened next.

Skykraft, the Canberra-based space services company, confirmed Bristol's board appointment on August 11 as it continues building out its satellite constellation for space-enabled ATM services. The company's pitch has always been technically compelling: a constellation of low-Earth orbit satellites providing space-based VHF voice and data communications alongside ADS-B surveillance, with global coverage that extends to oceanic and remote regions where ground-based VHF infrastructure simply doesn't reach.

## The Real Gap This Is Trying to Close

The communications problem Skykraft is targeting is old and genuinely frustrating for anyone who has flown or planned flights across oceanic tracks. <cite index="28-3,28-5,28-6">Voice radio communications in the VHF band are the standard exchange between pilots and air traffic controllers — but VHF services are only available when the aircraft is within range of a ground-based radio, which means vast portions of the Earth's surface, including most of the world's oceans, are simply not covered.</cite> CPDLC and HF radio have filled some of that gap over the years, but neither is seamless, and HF in particular has always been an operational workaround rather than a real solution.

<cite index="26-1">Skykraft's system is designed to provide global space-enabled ADS-B and VHF communications services</cite>, essentially replicating over-ocean what pilots and controllers take for granted near airports and over continental airspace. <cite index="28-1">A world-first trial of space-based VHF voice communications was successfully completed by Skykraft as part of their development program</cite>, and <cite index="25-2">the satellites provide voice radio communications in the VHF band between pilots and air traffic controllers anywhere on Earth.</cite>

That "anywhere" is the operative word. It's the same promise Aireon made with space-based ADS-B — and Aireon's trajectory (now consolidated under Iridium, as I covered in July) shows both how real the demand is and how long the path from demonstration to operational deployment actually runs.

## What the Board Appointment Is Really About

<cite index="20-4">Skykraft appointed former FAA ATO chief Teri Bristol to its board as it advances satellite-based VHF communications for global air traffic management.</cite> The choice of Bristol specifically is telling. The ATO isn't just an operational body — it's a major customer and standard-setter for any ATM infrastructure that touches US-managed airspace, including the oceanic regions the FAA coordinates over the North Atlantic and the Pacific. Getting that kind of regulatory and institutional credibility on the board suggests Skykraft is preparing for the kind of conversations that turn demonstration programs into contracted services with ANSPs.

That's the real underlying shift here. <cite index="26-3">The constellation aims to provide what would be the world's first full-service space-enabled air traffic management service</cite>, and reaching that milestone requires navigating not just technical certification but a complex web of ANSP relationships, ICAO standardization, and bilateral agreements between national authorities. Someone who has sat at the top of the FAA's operational side understands that landscape in a way a pure aerospace engineer does not.

From a flight-planning and cockpit perspective, the practical question isn't whether satellite-based VHF eventually works — the trials suggest it does. The question is how quickly it gets standardized into the procedures and avionics integration that make it usable in actual operations, and whether the eventual service model looks more like an Aireon-style infrastructure layer or a direct ANSP-contracted service. That distinction matters enormously for how the data and communications capability ultimately reaches the flight deck.

Skykraft is still in the early innings of commercial deployment, and there's a long way between a successful technical trial and global operational service. But the strategic moves it's making right now — constellation expansion, board composition, ANSP partnerships — look like a company that believes the window is opening.

questions: From a flight-planning standpoint, how much does the current VHF gap over oceanic tracks actually affect how you'd build a transatlantic or transpacific flight plan today — is it a genuine workflow pain point, or has CPDLC/HF mostly papered over it? (Genuine pain point / Mostly papered over / Somewhere in between)

Aireon proved that space-based surveillance can make the leap from demonstration to contracted ANSP service — but it took years and a heavyweight backer in Iridium. Does Skykraft's board move suggest they're trying to replicate that playbook, or do you read it as a different strategy? (Same playbook / Different approach / Too early to tell)

The board hire of an ex-FAA ATO chief is an obvious move for US market access, but Skykraft's near-term opportunity is arguably stronger in Asia-Pacific and oceanic airspace managed by non-US ANSPs. Do you think the US-regulatory credibility angle is the right priority at this stage, or would a non-US ANSP hire have sent a stronger commercial signal?
email_brief: Skykraft, an Australian startup building a low-Earth orbit satellite constellation for space-based ATM services (VHF voice/data comms and ADS-B surveillance), announced on August 11 that it has appointed Teri Bristol — former chief of the FAA's Air Traffic Organization — to its board of directors. The company has already completed world-first trials of satellite-based VHF voice between pilots and controllers and is working toward an operational global constellation. The appointment is notable because the core technology gap Skykraft targets — the absence of real VHF coverage over oceanic and remote airspace — directly affects how oceanic flight plans are built and how pilots communicate with ATC outside of radar and ground-radio coverage. This comes at a moment when space-based surveillance infrastructure (led by Aireon/Iridium, which we covered in July) is already establishing a commercial precedent, and the question is whether communications will follow the same trajectory from demonstration to contracted ANSP service.
